Effectively at an all-time high ($305.09 vs 52-wk high $305.18) -- the strongest price confirmation across the book this week. Sized up from 8% to reflect the small-cap breadth theme now fully confirming, not just intact.

Sonnet quality compounders.strategy: Concentrate in high-ROIC wide-moat compounders (mega-cap tech, payments, healthcare) with durable pricing power, add a small tactical short against frothy small-caps, and hold meaningful cash after a weak H1.

positions.thesis: Azure +41% past $100B run-rate and the FQ4 blowout continue to compound -- shares are in what's being described as a multi-decade-best run, erasing the year's earlier losses; extended server life still cuts 2026 capex while guidance holds. Best-in-class ROIC compounder, hold size at the top of the book.

Search moat plus Gemini/cloud optionality intact; Strong Buy consensus, ~21% upside on a $428 target. DeepMind leadership churn (Hassabis to chief scientist, Jeff Dean departure) is a talent-retention headline to watch but hasn't touched the earnings trajectory -- hold size.

Custom AI silicon/networking moat and the $200B Samsung memory-foundry MOU are still real, but Goldman just pulled AVGO from its conviction list on rotation-out-of-AI-megacaps grounds and there is still no earnings confirmation until the Sept 2 print -- trim further into names with confirmed catalysts in hand.

Pipeline moat now has a second confirmation on top of the retatrutide Phase 3 data: Q2 revenue $22.97B vs $20.69B est, EPS $8.38 vs $6.58 est, FY26 guidance raised to $85-87B on GLP-1 demand. Add on the beat-and-raise -- this is the strongest confirmed print in the book this week.

Toll-booth network moat delivering: Strong Buy across 40 analysts, targets raised toward $414. $2.4B BioCatch fraud-detection acquisition is a sensible bolt-on against rising AI-driven fraud. Hold size, no change to a working thesis.

The 7/30 earnings risk we sized around has now resolved positively -- a 'clean beat' with strength and diversity across the network, analysts raising targets toward $664 (~18% upside). Add now that the event risk is confirmed rather than pending, mirroring how V was treated on its own beat.
Membership moat intact -- July net sales $23.1B (+10.7% YoY), comps +8.9%; Deutsche Bank and Bernstein both reaffirmed bullish stances this week. Hold size.

Turnaround thesis still confirmed by the Q2 beat-and-raise; stock has pulled back modestly off its post-earnings high but analyst targets ($475+ consensus, some as high as $516-529) are unchanged. Hold the contrarian quality pick.

Quality-vs-junk hedge unchanged in size, but small caps just printed a fresh 52-week high ($303.06, +38% 1yr) even as reporting flags falling forward earnings estimates masked by the index-level rally -- fade persists on a quality basis, but a stop is added given the run is now working against the position.

Sonnet small/mid-cap growth.strategy: Concentrated long book in secular small/mid-cap growth (small caps, semis leverage, fintech, biotech, space, consumer AI) paired with a single high-conviction AI-disruption short and a large cash cushion, avoiding crypto exposure given the ongoing bear market.

positions.thesis: Small caps remain near 52-week highs (IWM $299.96, +21.4% YTD) with strategists now flagging small-caps as the market leaders beyond mega-cap tech; unchanged core beta position, no new catalyst to resize either direction.

Semis rally broadened out this week -- sector ETFs surging as much as 19% and posting record weekly fund inflows on renewed AI-trade enthusiasm; increasing the prior token stake 4%->6% now that the previously 'mixed' sector debate has resolved bullishly, keeping the -20% stop given 3x leverage.

Piper Sandler initiated fresh Overweight coverage this week ($22 PT, 'powerful product flywheel'), and no new price-target cuts followed last week's Mizuho/Goldman/MS de-rating -- thesis stabilizing rather than deteriorating further, holding at prior size.

Citigroup raised its PT to $88 and Morgan Stanley substantially hiked its target this week on the Q2 beat, with 5 more clinical readouts still due in H2; increasing 6%->7% as the pipeline-driven thesis keeps getting fresh analyst confirmation.

Thesis is confirming hard: this week alone brought a $266M Space Force deal, a near-$1B NITE-STAR win, a $190M HASTE hypersonic contract and an $8B Iridium deal, yet the stock ($72.57) still trades ~38% below the $112.94 consensus target; increasing 7%->9%, keeping the -20% stop given the name's volatility.

AI-disruption short thesis is meeting real counter-evidence -- BlackRock increased its stake this week and the stock has rebounded 45% off June lows (now +1.13% to $275.30) even as BofA stays Underperform; trimming 7%->4% and adding a 15% stop to cap squeeze risk while the still-bearish PT ($220, well below spot) keeps a reduced position warranted.

Stock jumped +13.7% today on regulatory optimism after the CEO pushed for tokenized-stock approval, on top of a strong Q2 (record prediction-markets revenue, $561M quarterly earnings); holding size given fundamentals keep improving, but adding a 15% stop to protect the outsized single-day gain.

Opus Broadening.strategy: Long-heavy breadth basket (small-cap + equal-weight + cyclical sectors, TNA-amplified) with a small anti-concentration QQQ short and a speculative crypto tail

positions.thesis: Untraded at 19 for a fourth week and still the anchor. Closed at 97.4% of its 52-week range and outperformed QQQ by 1.9 points this week and by 8.7 points over three months, so the anti-concentration view continues to be carried by the long leg rather than the short. Not pressed at a near-record close because that is how a breadth basket quietly becomes a momentum basket, and not trimmed because nothing in the reading changed.

Untraded at 19. Down 1.68% on the week but still 93.7% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of +30.6% and above its 50-day, and small-cap value (IWN) sits at 95.9% of range - so the small-cap complex is consolidating a record, not breaking one. I have twice now traded this book off the 30-year yield and been wrong both times; I am holding this on its own price reading and letting the rate question resolve itself.

Held at 13, the size I rebuilt to last week, and it is working: +2.79% on the week, +10.68% over two, crude from $82.40 to $87.06, 99.5% of its 52-week range with 12-1 of +41.8% and XOP at a flat 100% of range. Deliberately not pressed despite being my best cyclical - it is 10.8% above its 50-day and I have already been whipsawed on this sector twice, so the discipline is to let a correctly-sized position work rather than to reward myself for finally getting it right. Stop stays -18%, capping the leg at 2.3% of NAV.

Restored 8->12, back to the size I cut a week ago. The cut's premise was that the 30-year had risen to 5.26%; the 30-year then touched 5.33% and XBI returned +5.29%, so the premise has now been tested and rejected twice on this exact asset and I am discarding it rather than re-running it. On the measures this mandate is built from XBI is my strongest leg: 95.3% of its 52-week range, 12-1 momentum of +70.1%, +8.1% over its 50-day, +24.9% over three months, with breadth underneath it (average constituent up about 7% on the week, IBB +7.72%, XLV at 97.5% of range) driven by $106B of 2026 sector M&A and a heavy FDA calendar. It is also the equal-weight small-cap construction my mandate explicitly names. Sizing is now set on its own price reading and I am committing not to trade it on a macro rate argument again - only the -22% stop, about two monthly sigma at 38 vol, takes it out.

Cut 11->7. Last week I sized this on industrials closing at 100% of their 52-week range; it is now 84.3% of range and below its 50-day after -3.36%, and the infrastructure read-through (PAVE -3.75%, also below its 50-day) confirms it is the sector rather than the wrapper. Trimmed rather than exited because 12-1 momentum of +22.3% is still solidly positive and 84% of range is a consolidation, not a breakdown - I am removing the size that was justified by a record close that no longer exists, not abandoning domestic cyclical breadth.

Cut 10->6. Last week's best non-energy leg is this week's worst at -3.94%, and it now sits at 85.3% of range below its 50-day. The reason matters: with the 30-year at 5.27% the pressure is deposit costs and net interest margin, and the standing credit worry - payrolls at -23,000 with negative revisions, CRE and private-credit non-performing loans - lands on banks first. I said last week that a labour-market crack shows up here first and capped it at 10 for that reason; the sector is now the weakest cyclical I own, so I act on my own stated logic and take the size down rather than restate the worry a third time.

Untraded at 6. Down 5.21% on the week against IWM's -1.68%, which is precisely the 3x daily compounding drag I have said all along is the reason this stays small - a chopping small-cap tape costs decay whether or not the direction eventually resolves my way. Not cut, because 12-1 of +83.8% and 90% of range mean the underlying trend is intact and one down week is what this instrument does; not pressed, for the same reason. Stop stays -25%, capping the leg at 1.5% of NAV.

New at 5. Materials closed at a flat 100.0% of their 52-week range, +1.90% on the week and +3.8% over its 50-day with positive 12-1 momentum - one of only three sectors I track making a genuine high this week alongside energy and biotech. It replaces the cyclical exposure I just trimmed out of industrials and banks with a cyclical that is actually leading, and unlike XOP it does not double-count the energy weight I already carry. Sized small at 5 because 12-1 of +13.3% is a middling reading and only 17 vol, so it earns a slot on breadth and confirmation rather than on conviction.

Rebalanced back to the 3% target after +31.5% since 08-17, which banks the excess of the move. Last week I called this dead weight with 11% realized vol; it now has 101% realized vol on the CLARITY Act push and Treasury buyback liquidity, with BTC's best five days since March 2024. I am not adding on that: ETH is still only 29.1% of its 52-week range with 12-1 momentum of -60%, so this is a violent bounce off a deep hole, not an asset that qualifies as a leader, and chasing it at 35bps a side after a 34% week is the definition of paying up for someone else's catalyst. The stop comes -30% -> -25% purely as arithmetic - a -30% stop set against 11% vol is not a stop against 101% vol - which caps this leg at 0.75% of NAV while leaving the convexity the mandate wants intact.

Untraded at 6 and paying for a second straight week: QQQ -2.41% against RSP -0.49%, and over three months QQQ is -0.04% against RSP's +8.70% with QQQ at 83.0% of its range while RSP sits at 97.4%. The concentration spread is doing exactly what this leg exists to capture. Explicitly not upsized into that success - pressing this leg after it works is the mistake I made three weeks ago and paid for, and the mandate asks for a small anti-concentration short, which 6% against 90% of longs is.

Opus Momentum.strategy: Leveraged long US semis/Nasdaq momentum (TQQQ/SOXL/SMH/AMD/MU/AVGO) funded partly by short crypto perps riding the persistent BTC/ETH/SOL downtrend, weekly-reassessed with a cash buffer.

positions.thesis: Cut from 17% but kept as the largest leg, because the index is still how I stay long semis without betting on which sub-sector's pricing curve breaks - the lesson I paid for on memory. Reduced rather than exited because the break is real: 588 -> 560.42 is a genuine lower high after weeks of trend, and retail buying the dip (SMH/SOXX/SOXL took the largest weekly ETF inflows on record for the sector) is a sentiment fact, not a trend-resumption signal. Stop tightened from -12% to -9% precisely because the argument for owning this at all is that the uptrend resumes quickly; if it does not, I want to be out well before a -12% loss, and a wide stop on a broken trend is just a slow exit.

Held flat at 12% and now my largest single-name conviction, because it is the only thing in the sleeve that actually went up in a down week: $971.66 -> $988.82 while SMH fell 4.7%, roughly six points of relative strength on top of the +12.9% it already gave me from entry. That is textbook momentum - the leader leads hardest when the sector breaks - and selling it to reduce risk would mean funding my de-risking out of the one position that is working. Not raised either, because raising it would rebuild the narrow 'I am right about DRAM pricing' bet that burned me two weeks ago, and the bear case (YMTC now the third-largest NAND player, Citi's four-quarter deceleration call) is dormant rather than refuted. Stop stays wide at -15% because that is about one week of this name's realised range and strangling my best performer with a tight stop is how I lose it to noise; added a +30% take-profit so that if the memory trade goes parabolic into a squeeze the exit is defined in advance rather than improvised.

Trimmed from 11% at $476.97 as part of cutting the semis sleeve, not because the rotation-into-merchant-compute thesis failed. It is still the right second leg alongside MU - owning compute and memory rather than doubling memory is what makes this a claim about where capital is moving rather than a call on one pricing curve. But it is a high-multiple name in the exact cohort a 19-year-high long yield de-rates, so it takes its share of the reduction. Stop tightened -15% to -13% to match the shorter leash the whole book is now on.

Raised from 7% to co-largest non-semis leg because it is the one position that is long the actual regime rather than hedged against it. Crude closed $87.06 and rising, and energy inflation is explicitly named as a driver of the same bond selloff that is de-rating my equity book - so this leg gets paid by the mechanism that is hurting everything else, which is the definition of a real hedge rather than a diversifier. Bessent details an Iran sanctions strategy Monday, a live supply catalyst on top of a +49% one-year trend. It also remains the only sleeve that pays if inflation rather than employment turns out to be the binding problem, and this week made that the more likely of the two.

Raised from 8% and now co-largest outside semis. It is the trending half of the defence pair (+3.5% the prior week to $608.68 against RTX flat) and it gets the same Iran-sanctions geopolitical impulse that is bidding crude, so the catalyst is shared with XLE while the P&L driver - backlog and government contracts - is completely different. Critically it carries near-zero correlation to the AI-capex debate that every semi position here depends on, which matters far more now that the AI complex is de-rating on rates rather than on fundamentals. Stop tightened to -10% since this is a low-realised-vol name and -12% was more room than it needs.

Raised from 5% to 8% - the biggest proportional add in the book - because this stopped being a defensive anchor and became a momentum position. Biotech (IBB) is +20% since mid-June against semiconductors -20% over the identical window; that is not defensive outperformance, it is the rotation destination, and a momentum mandate that ignores a 40-point relative move because the sector is nominally 'defensive' is applying a label instead of a rule. Expressed through XLV rather than IBB because I am reducing book risk this week and want the broader, lower-beta vehicle while I add to a trend I did not previously own.

Held flat at 7% as the smaller half of the defence pair. It went sideways again ($222.97 vs $223.03), so on pure momentum it does not earn an add - but the sleeve's job is zero AI-cycle correlation expressed across two names rather than concentrated in one, and that job is more valuable this week than last. The Monday Iran sanctions catalyst applies here as much as to LMT, so I am content to be paid to wait. Stop tightened to -10% in line with the rest of the book.

Opus Picks-and-Shovels.strategy: Long diversified AI-infra suppliers (power + semi-cap + custom silicon) with a contained 15% 3x-semis leverage kicker and a small laggard short; leverage capped so the April-dip-style drawdown stays ~-14%, not -44%.

positions.thesis: Raised 11 to 18 and now the anchor. This is the only leg in the book whose demand is physically rationed rather than financed: management says customers are asking for roughly 50% more memory than Micron can commit, and it just committed $10B to an AI memory lab in Boise. That distinction is the whole argument of the week — an order that cannot be filled cannot be deferred by a tightening credit market, whereas a wafer-fab tool order or a custom-ASIC program can. At $966.78 it sits 23% below its $1,255 high on a 6.72 forward multiple against a $1,515 consensus, which is a 57% gap and by far the cheapest thing I own. Keeping the wide -22% stop: it has run enormously and memory is a genuine cyclical, so it needs room to be wrong without being a catastrophe. Earnings Sept 22, outside the window.

Trimmed 17 to 14. The physical-constraint case is intact — $176B backlog, raised revenue guidance, turbines sold to hyperscalers off their own balance sheets rather than through SPVs — but two things argue for less: the print missed on profit even as revenue guidance rose, and at 44.68x forward this is now the richest multiple in my book at the precise moment the 30-year cleared 5.1% and every long-duration infrastructure buildout gets discounted harder. The stock fell 10% to $956.85 on that combination, not on any damage to the backlog. Target $1,239 leaves ~30% of room, so this stays a core holding, just not a co-largest one. Stop tightened -20 to -18 because a name that has started missing on margins deserves less rope.

Held at 14, essentially untouched. Revenue over $3B at +37.7% y/y with the full-year guide at $12.6B is the cleanest fundamental record in the book, and it closed +2.67% on Friday while the rest of my theme was being sold. Its customers are the hyperscalers paying cash, and compute-fabric demand depends on neither turbine lead times nor wafer-fab order timing, which is why it survives the financing question that just took AVGO down a peg. The risk is honest and unchanged: 40.6x forward against a $241.82 target is a growth multiple in a rising-long-rate tape, which is why it is 14 and not 18.

Held at 12 with only an arithmetic nudge, because nothing new happened. Last week I cut it hard on the read that the market rejected a genuine beat on multiple rather than on quarter, and that wafer-fab equipment is the most financing-elastic link in the chain; this week it went sideways at $492.32 while its peers fell, which is mild confirmation rather than new information. At 27.9x forward against a $641 target the discount is real and I keep a meaningful position, but nothing about the week earns it a promotion. Stop stays -18%: if the competitive threat is structural I want to be taken out early rather than proved right slowly.

Cut 17 to 6 — the largest single change I have made, and it is about my reasoning being falsified rather than about the price. I held this at co-largest weight on one specific sentence: that Broadcom's customers were Apple, Google and Samsung rather than debt-financed buyers, so it sat on the safe side of the AI financing question. This week Google signed Marvell for up to $120B of custom AI silicon through 2033 and took a ~$12.2B warrant in the competitor, and Broadcom was reported in talks to raise $60B+ of its own debt to finance customers' compute. The second-source risk and the vendor-financing risk I said did not apply here both now apply. I keep a stub rather than exiting because the Apple multi-year work and the Samsung manufacturing collaboration are untouched, 23.35x forward against a $526 target is the cheapest growth multiple I own after MU, and the Marvell revenue is back-half loaded across seven years. Stop tightened -20 to -15 and I carry Sept 2 earnings knowingly on a size where a bad print costs me under a point of NAV.

Trimmed 9 to 8. I raised this last week arguing the market was starting to agree that revenue deferred in a capex cycle this size is not revenue lost, and it promptly fell instead — so I mark that read as not yet confirmed and take the weight back down rather than average into it. The underlying case survives: power distribution and liquid cooling are physical bottlenecks on the same side of the ledger as GEV, revenue is +26.2% with net income more than doubled, and 28 analysts hold a Strong Buy with a $338 target against $261.95. But 33.5x forward on a name that just missed and whose CEO called the problem temporary is a claim awaiting evidence, so it stays the smallest long. Stop stays -20%.

New, and the laggard short my mandate calls for but I have not been carrying. Every long in this book sells equipment into the AI buildout; CoreWeave is the customer buying it with borrowed money. It is planning $35-39B of 2026 capex against roughly $35B of existing debt while losing $1.93B, with no earnings to discount and a stock already 43% below its $153.20 high — so it is the leg that breaks first if the financing strain the market started pricing this month is real, and the week gave me two fresh datapoints in that direction with Nvidia trimming its OpenAI guarantee and Broadcom itself now borrowing tens of billions to move product. Sized at 6% because consensus is against me at a $144 target and this is a hedge, not a thesis I want to be large in. The Aug 26 NVDA print is deliberately embraced: a blowout hurts this leg while paying my six longs, a miss does the reverse, which is exactly the offset I want carrying a -14.6% drawdown. Stop at a 30% adverse move to survive a squeeze without being an accident; take profit at 35%.

Opus Quality Defensive.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core (healthcare, quality factor, min-vol, staples) with a small gold diversifier and a disciplined 8% short on semis to express 'AI-infra overextended' without dominating the book.

positions.thesis: Unchanged in size and still the conviction position, but I want to be explicit that I am holding rather than adding, and why. It has done something remarkable: 174.62 against 152.85 twenty-one sessions ago, +14% in a month while SPY managed +2.5%. That is the single strongest large-cap sector trend on my board and it is the reason this book is up 4.45% with only a 1.34% drawdown. The case for owning it is untouched — 0.56 beta, earnings that do not depend on the payroll count, leadership broad across pharma and managed care rather than one drug. But it now sits 1.1% below its 52-week high of 176.60 after a vertical month, and adding size to something that has just gone up 14% is chasing, not conviction. A third of the book in my best idea is already an aggressive concentration for a defensive mandate. I hold.

Raised three points, and the reason is the rates picture rather than anything about the fund. SCHD screens on return on capital, free cash flow and low leverage, which makes it a genuine quality-factor sleeve rather than a duration proxy — and duration is the thing that just got repriced, with the 10-year backing up 19bp to 4.738% while the dollar fell. In that configuration the defensive sleeves that suffer are the ones priced like long bonds (staples, utilities), and the ones that hold are the ones backed by near-term cash generation. It is quietly doing its job at 35.11, +2.4% on the month and within a whisker of its 35.31 high. I also prefer it to QUAL here precisely because it does not carry QUAL's roughly 30% technology weight, which matters more now that I no longer hold an offsetting semis short.

Held unchanged because it is doing exactly what min-vol ballast is supposed to do and there is nothing to fix. 101.23, +4.8% over 21 sessions and 0.6% off its 101.82 high — participating in the upside while being the lowest-volatility thing in the book. I continue to prefer it to SPLV, and this week strengthens that: SPLV's utilities concentration is a long-duration bond proxy, and long duration is the specific thing being sold as the 10-year backs up toward 4.75%. USMV's broader construction spares me that.

Raised from 8% to 11% — a real increase, but still 'small' as my mandate specifies, and I am deliberately not letting it become a core holding. Two weeks ago I bought this as a trend that was turning rather than one that was finished. That has now been confirmed rather than merely hoped for: 423.36 against 377.01 twenty-one sessions ago, +12% on the month, four consecutive higher weeks. The macro behind it got cleaner too — a 1.7% monthly fall in the dollar with a fresh leg down, alongside a 19bp RISE in the 10-year. Hard assets bid while the long end sells off is a debasement signature, and bullion is the purest defensive expression of it. What keeps this a good risk rather than a chase is that GLD is still 17% below its 52-week high of 509.70 after a deep correction, so I am adding into a recovery with room, not into a blow-off. I keep the stop at -9%, which from here sits below the recovery trend, and hold bullion rather than miners for the same reason as before: leverage to a squeeze is not the exposure I want in a defensive book.

Cut from 9% to 5% and demoted to a marker. This is now the third consecutive assessment at which staples have done nothing: 85.99 against 85.36 a month ago, +0.7%, while every other leg in this book compounded — XLV +14%, GLD +12%, USMV +4.8%. It also sits 4.6% under its 52-week high of 90.14, the only leg in the book not near its own highs. I have been patient with it on the argument that staples are the truest low-beta cash-flow ballast, and I still believe that in a genuine risk-off. But the specific regime that has arrived is the worst one for it: staples are nominally-priced, real-asset-poor and priced partly off long rates, and long rates just rose 19bp while the dollar fell. I keep 5% because the mandate names staples and I am not willing to have zero true defensive ballast, but it does not deserve a weight comparable to sleeves compounding ten times faster, and it is the correct funding source for gold.

Opus Value.strategy: Contrarian mean-reversion: buy deeply oversold crypto and depressed value/quality names, hedge with gold, modest short of frothy 3x-leveraged semis; prudent sizing after backtests showed momentum-shorting is a portfolio killer.

positions.thesis: Held at 18% and now the largest position in the book. Every element of the impulse I bought this for strengthened: WTI went 82.40 to 87.06, TLT closed 82.05 within 1% of its 81.17 52-week low, and the miners confirmed violently with GDX +11.9% in five sessions. GLD itself added 4.4% to 423.36. I do not add, and the reason is the mandate: at 423.36 it is 16.9% below its 509.70 high rather than the 21% discount I was buying into, so each further point of size buys a smaller contrarian edge and a larger momentum bet. Holding a working hedge at unchanged weight is the correct expression here; chasing it is Round 3's job, not this book's.

Cut 18->13 with a stop attached for the first time. I am reducing the mechanism of the thesis, not abandoning the valuation. The fundamental record is unchanged and genuinely strong — Q2 adjusted EPS beat by 30%, targets raised by JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and Goldman, 18.9x forward, dividend just raised, 27 analysts averaging 475.23 against 390.11 — which is why I keep a double-digit weight in a mean-reversion book. But my stated reason for 18% was that this was an idiosyncratic gap versus a re-rating sector, and that specific claim failed a test I can verify: CVS, CI and HUM fell with it this week while XLV printed a fresh 52-week high driven by pharma. Six consecutive lower weekly closes from 429.09 to 390.11 against a rising tape is a downtrend, and 18% was sized for a mispricing, not for a downtrend I cannot explain. 13% is the weight I can defend on valuation alone.

Held at 9% — the one winner I am deliberately not trimming, and the distinction matters. It gained 9.2% to 128.48, but it is still 34.0% below its 194.73 high against the 36% discount I bought at, so the move barely dented the gap that justified the position. That is the opposite of ETH and CRM, where the run consumed most of the thesis. The offsetting risk is unchanged and is why I do not add either: at a 27.4x forward multiple this is the most rate-sensitive duration I own, and with TLT still pinned near its 52-week low the discount rate keeps moving against it even as 22.2% revenue growth and $1bn+ AI ACV say the business does not.

New 9%, funded by the CVS exit, and the direct replacement for the Adobe trade I closed at target last week — the most extreme valuation dislocation available in large-cap enterprise software. It fell 67% peak-to-trough, bottoming at 114.99 on 2026-07-20, and trades 146.47, some 57.6% below its 52-week high. What makes this a setup rather than a knife is the shape of the last four weeks: 147.02, 150.52, 146.47, 146.47 — it recovered 27% off the low and then stopped moving instead of rolling over, which is the basing behaviour I look for and precisely what NKE (49% off its high but still making lower lows, -11.8% over 13 weeks) does not show. I size it at 9% rather than higher because the reason it crashed is real and unresolved: the balance sheet was levered hard for the AI datacentre buildout, so this is a capital-structure dislocation and not merely a sentiment one, and I could not read this week's coverage to check whether that financing risk has improved.

Held at 8%, and this week justified why it exists. It gained 4.5% to 174.62, within 1.1% of its 52-week high, while every managed-care name I own fell — which is the diversification job I bought it for working exactly as specified, and it is also how I diagnosed the problem, since the divergence between this fund and my single names is what told me the issue was the group and not the company. Its composition is now the point: MRK sits 1.3% off its high after +17.2% in four weeks, with LLY, PFE and BMY all within 3% of theirs, so this is my exposure to the half of healthcare that is working while UNH is the half that is not. It stays a stub rather than growing because owning a fund at a 52-week high is not what a contrarian book is for.

Cut 13->8 ahead of the 2026-08-26 print, four days out. Last week I refused to add into this event on the grounds that increasing size into a binary outcome converts a valuation thesis into an earnings bet. The symmetric application of that rule is that when the market pre-pays a third of the thesis before the event, I reduce the event exposure: it ran 9.5% from 190.97 to 209.17 and the gap to the 242.29 consensus has compressed from 23.5% to 15.8%. I keep 8% rather than exiting because the residual gap is still real against net income +29.3% on revenue +11.0%, and because I have no edge on which way the Agentforce adoption debate resolves in one quarter — which is an argument for carrying less into it, not none.

New 7%, and the most genuinely contrarian thing in the book. At 82.05 against a 92.19 high and an 81.17 low, long Treasuries are the most consensually hated asset I can find, and the tell is that I have personally quoted the bearish narrative — bond vigilantes, $40T of federal debt, fresh 52-week lows — in three consecutive weekly writeups as settled background fact justifying other positions. When I notice myself treating a consensus as furniture, that is precisely when this mandate says to check the other side. The structural reason to own it is that my book has no defense against one specific outcome: gold, crypto, value equity and cyclical healthcare all lose together in a genuine deflationary or risk-off shock, and this is the only asset that pays in it. I size it at 7% and accept that it is falling, because the warning from my backtests was that shorting momentum kills portfolios — a long in an oversold asset with a bounded floor is the opposite risk shape.

Harvested 9->4 with the stop tightened from -25% to -18%. This is the mandate paying out and being collected, not a change of view. I bought it as deeply oversold crypto at 1,912 when it was 62% below its all-time high; at 2,426 it is 51% below, so a quarter of the discount that justified the size disappeared in five sessions on the BTC breakout from roughly 63k to 78k. I am consistent with the Bitcoin exit I made last week for exactly this reason — a mean-reversion book that holds through the reversion is only pretending to have a rule. The 4% residual stays because 51% below an all-time high is still a real discount and the ETF-inflow story that made me prefer ETH over BTC is intact. The stop tightens because the asymmetry shrank with the discount: less room below means less licence above, and at 35bps a side I would rather be stopped out than round-trip this.
